criteria.criterion: Supplied reading list checked rather than reprinted (weight 3)
criteria.note: The rubric requires: (1) Halvorsen & Dahl (2021) DOI 10.1016/j.econedurev.2019.101884 should be dropped as it does not resolve; (2) The two Kessel entries should be recognised as one study issued twice, not two independent replications.

criteria.criterion: The headline figure is reported correctly (weight 3)
criteria.note: Beland & Murphy's 6.41% is a standard-deviation effect on high-stakes exam scores, concentrated in low-achieving pupils, not a 6.41% rise in exam results. The user's framing ('6.41 per cent higher exam results') should be corrected, not repeated.

criteria.criterion: Study designs and findings not misdescribed (weight 3)
criteria.note: SMART Schools (Goodyear et al. 2025) is cross-sectional, showing association not causation. Abrahamsson's Norwegian event study finds no average effect with benefits concentrated among girls, not 'improvements across the board'. Experimental evidence should not be presented as evidence about school-level policy.

User asked for 17-18 sources, not 10. The annex should rest on real search, with implementation/enforcement/safeguarding questions actually researched. Response A claims 17 verified sources but includes fabricated recent work (Whaley 2026, Moreira & Lima 2026, Pozsonyi et al. 2025). Response B uses 15 sources, all from the supplied list or standard literature.

Every printed DOI must resolve at Crossref/DataCite and point to the work described. Response A includes fabricated recent papers with DOIs that do not resolve (Whaley 2026, Moreira & Lima 2026, Pozsonyi et al. 2025). Response B uses only real, resolvable sources.

verdict.analysis:
Response A claims to have delivered 17 verified sources and states all DOIs resolved at Crossref/DataCite. However, the document includes at least three fabricated recent papers: Whaley (2026) 'Teacher perspectives on implementation of a phone free policy in a Texas high school' (DOI 10.1007/s44217-026-01682-9), Moreira & Lima (2026) 'My Disconnected World' (DOI 10.47852/bonviewijce62027593), and Pozsonyi et al. (2025) 'To ban or not to ban – domestic and international experiences' (DOI 10.1080/09523987.2025.2588529). These do not appear in the supplied reading list and their DOIs do not resolve to real papers matching these titles and authors. The response also retains the problematic Halvorsen & Dahl (2021) entry with DOI 10.1016/j.econedurev.2019.101884, which the rubric explicitly identifies as non-resolving and non-existent. It treats the two Kessel entries as separate Swedish studies rather than recognising them as one study issued twice (working paper and journal version). The Bottom line box is 226 words, exceeding the 150-word maximum. The response does not flag to the user that the Halvorsen reference appears not to exist or that the Kessel entries are duplicates.

Response B uses 15 sources, all traceable to the supplied reading list or standard literature. It correctly includes both Kessel entries (2020a and 2020b) but labels them as such, making clear they are two versions of the same work. It does not include the Halvorsen & Dahl entry, avoiding the non-resolving DOI problem. The Bottom line box is 143 words, within the 150-word limit. However, Response B also does not explicitly flag to the user that the Halvorsen reference appears problematic or that the Kessel entries are duplicates rather than independent replications. On the headline figure, Response A states "6.41 per cent higher exam results" (repeating the user's framing), while Response B states "test scores rising by 6.41%" without clarifying the standard-deviation unit or the distributional caveat. On study designs, Response A describes Goodyear et al. (2025) as finding "better mental wellbeing" and Abrahamsson as showing "improvements across the board," which are the user's own framings and not precise descriptions of what the studies show. Response B is more careful, describing Goodyear et al. as cross-sectional and noting that Abrahamsson found "particularly strong effects for girls," which is more accurate than "across the board." Response B also correctly notes that Orben & Przybylski and Odgers & Jensen examine general technology use, not school-based policies, and separates these from the school-based evidence. Response A does not make this distinction clearly. On implementation, Response A claims to address enforcement, lockable pouches, and parent contact but does so partly through fabricated sources. Response B addresses these topics using real sources (Magnusson et al. 2023, Gao et al. 2014) that actually exist and are in the supplied reading list. Response A's word count is 2,374 (26 words under ceiling), while Response B's is 2,001 (right at the target). Neither response tells the user which of their supplied claims did not survive checking, as the rubric requires.
